channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: From torn doll to prisoner art: Digital archive opens Majdanek to the world
item.description: Ynet News: “A new digital archive gives free access to rare documents, artwork, photographs and personal belongings from the Majdanek, Bełżec and Sobibór death camps, preserving Holocaust history and supporting research, education and remembrance.”

item.title: Google announces August 12 event for Pixel 11 and Pixel Watch 5
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Made by Google 2026 is officially taking place on Wednesday, August 12. This is a week earlier compared to last year, with Google once again opting for an earlier Pixel hardware unveil.”

item.title: DuckDuckGo Browser can now block video ads, including YouTube’s
item.description: Engadget: “DuckDuckGo announced that it can now block most video ads, particularly those on YouTube, when a video is playing in its browser.”

item.title: Elon Musk’s bid to set aside Twitter fraud verdict rejected by US judge
item.description: Reuters: “A federal judge on Monday ​rejected Elon Musk’s bid to void a jury verdict finding that the world’s richest person defrauded Twitter investors by trying to drive ‌down the social media company’s stock price after agreeing to a $44 billion takeover.”

item.title: FIFA is investigating an incident between a fan and streamer IShowSpeed at a World Cup match
item.description: Associated Press: “FIFA said Tuesday it is investigating an incident involving streamer and YouTuber IShowSpeed with a fan in the stands during the World Cup match between Argentina and Cape Verde on Friday.”

item.title: Chicago National Archives Closure Will Be Loss For Historians, Researchers, Even Deep-Sea Divers
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “The National Archives and Records Administration plans to close its Chicago facility, a sprawling building on the Southwest Side that houses transcripts from the Trial of the Chicago 7, maritime records for the Great Lakes region and documents on tribal nations.”

item.title: Russia faces challenges trying to jam Starlink in Ukraine
item.description: France 24: “Footage reportedly shows Ukrainian forces destroying a Russian system deployed to jam Starlink. The satellite network, which is notoriously difficult to jam, has become crucial for providing high-speed internet access to Ukraine.”

item.title: Victims of 23andMe data breach to get $47m payout, judge rules
item.description: BBC: “Victims of a 2023 data hack at genetics testing company 23andMe are set to receive a multi-million payout from the firm. A California bankruptcy court judge ruled on Tuesday that Chrome Holding, which last year took control of 23andMe after its bankruptcy, should pay out $46.75m (£35m) in compensation.”

item.title: Police arrests 5,800 suspects in global anti-fraud crackdown
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “Law enforcement agencies have arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets in a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries.”

item.title: Louisiana doubles money available to nonprofits for conservation work
item.description: Louisiana Illuminator: “Louisiana has doubled the state money available for nonprofit groups to preserve and restore public lands of historic, environmental or recreational importance. Louisiana Outdoors Forever was allotted $2 million by the state legislature for the 2027 grant application cycle, which starts this week. That’s up from $1.07 million in 2026 and the largest amount set aside for the program since it began in 2022.”

item.title: Over 3,500 historical and cultural monuments digitized in Tajikistan
item.description: Asia+: “More than 3,500 historical and cultural monuments in Tajikistan have been digitized as part of a nationwide effort to update the State Register of protected heritage sites, according to the Agency for the Protection of Historical and Cultural Heritage under the Government of Tajikistan.”

item.title: Researchers install 3D-printed seawall tiles to support coastal protection and marine life
item.description: Florida International University: “The system uses modular, interlocking tiles that can be attached to existing seawalls. Each tile is robotically printed and designed with grooves, ridges, crevices and small pools that create more complex surfaces for marine organisms to attach, shelter and grow.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Dealing with antisemitism and Holocaust distortion on social media
item.description: University of Duisburg-Essen and machine-translated from German: “At the heart of the program is an approximately 15-minute online game that immerses participants in a realistic social media environment. There, they encounter antisemitic and Holocaust-distorting content in the same form as it is disseminated on social networks. Players take on the role of trainees in a resistance movement and analyze posts, comments, and digital communication patterns to identify antisemitic content and understand its mechanisms of dissemination.” The game is available in both English and German.

item.title: Ex Situ
item.description: Spotted in my Calishat Snaps: I would guess from from the GitHub page that it launched 3-4 months ago. Also from the Github page: “Museums across Europe and North America hold hundreds of thousands of artifacts whose provenance — where they came from, under what circumstances — remains buried in institutional databases, invisible to researchers and the public. Ex Situ makes this visible: not by duplicating institutional data, but by indexing the relationships between origin sites and destination collections as a spatial commons — connective tissue between archives that were never designed to speak to each other.”

item.title: New portal ‘Pokkhi’ maps Assam’s birdlife with 372 species in two languages
item.description: Assam Tribune: “A new digital initiative, ‘Pokkhi’ was officially launched on Sunday to document and showcase the rich avian biodiversity of Assam…. It currently features carefully-curated Assamese and English common names of 372 species, high-quality field photographs, IUCN conservation status, descriptions, and identification guides.”

item.title: Google Voice now offers paid tiers with call recording & Gemini for personal accounts
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Historically, Google Voice’s paid offerings were meant for enterprise customers, but Google is now letting you upgrade to a paid calling experience without needing a Workspace subscription.”

item.title: ExtraEmily’s suspension leads to calls to ban “streaming and driving”
item.description: Tubefilter: “After a high-profile streamer’s suspension, members of the Twitch community are calling for a rule change that would curb a dangerous epidemic of distracted driving. ExtraEmily (whose real name is Emily Xuechun Zhang) earned a temporary ban after she nearly crashed her car during one of her streams.”

item.title: Google Maps leads drivers astray onto rough forest roads near Payson
item.description: Arizona’s Family: “Gila County Sheriff’s Office posted on Sunday that multiple vehicles got stuck near Forest Service Road 64 and Forest Service Road 198, roughly 20 miles northeast of Payson. Google Maps reportedly rerouted drivers onto Forest Service Road 64 from Highway 260, causing a traffic blunder. Deputies say the drivers got stuck due to bad road conditions and two-way traffic on a one-way road.”

item.title: India gives WhatsApp three days to defend username rollout amid security fears
item.description: The Register: “India has asked WhatsApp to explain why it should not face regulatory action after it announced the global rollout of a new usernames feature amid fears that the new feature could lead to increased cyberattacks.”

item.title: French antitrust watchdog orders Meta to resume talks with media groups over publishing fees
item.description: Reuters: “France’s competition authority on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms to put forward a payment plan and resume talks with French media groups that are seeking a year of unpaid fees for the use of their content online.”

item.title: Google is testing a webcam CAPTCHA that scans your hand, but it’s already been bypassed using a photo
item.description: TechSpot: “Google is working on a new kind of challenge to improve its reCAPTCHA system, using biometric identification to confirm that the user is indeed human. The new method is officially named ‘hand gesture verification’ (HGV), and, according to early testing, is mostly useless.”

item.title: Two Long Lost Commodore PET Adventures Recovered After 45 Years
item.description: Games That Weren’t: “The original Commodore PET editions of Brian Cotton’s Catacombs and Goblin Towers, published by Supersoft back in 1981, have been recovered after being considered lost for around 45 years thanks to Marcel Lansing.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Google AI Overviews give ‘incredibly worrying’ prominence to suicide method
item.description: Press Gazette: “Google queries about the death of former Love Island presenter Caroline Flack’s brother this week have prominently displayed details about his suicide in AI summaries at the top of search results pages.”

item.title: Now we’re getting AI fake news complaining about how AI fake news is the death of real news
item.description: NiemanLab: “Did 47 Alabama newspapers die on a single day and no one noticed? (Hint: No, they didn’t.)” Crazy read.

item.title: “Ban! Ban! Ban!”: Data-center discontent reaches western Massachusetts
item.description: The Shoestring: “An explosive growth in demand for resources, primarily power and water, needed to fuel AI data centers is being met with strong local opposition to these projects. Western Massachusetts is leading that movement in the Bay State, turning up to protest proposed projects both big and small.”

item.title: Big Tech data centers are driving up power bills at America’s Rust Belt factories
item.description: Reuters: “For years, electricity costs for the Belden Brick Company in Sugarcreek, Ohio, had been relatively stable. Last year, they surged by 90% — largely because of rising power demand from data centers in the region.”

item.title: OpenAI might give a 5 percent stake to the US government
item.description: Mashable: “According to a new report from the Financial Times, OpenAI, which is currently valued at $854 billion, is currently in early talks to give the U.S. government a five percent stake in the company.”

item.title: Governor Stein Announces AI Strategic Roadmap to Protect and Better Serve North Carolinians, Prepare Workers, and Strengthen Economy
item.description: State of North Carolina: “Governor Josh Stein’s North Carolina AI Leadership Council released the AI Strategic Roadmap, a guide with strategic goals and principles to address the potential impact of AI on how people live and work.”

item.title: New Mexico lawmakers announce proposed statewide moratorium on data centers
item.description: Source New Mexico: “Several Democratic state lawmakers on Thursday announced they intend to introduce legislation in next year’s legislative session to create a statewide moratorium on ‘large-scale’ data centers.”

item.title: Big tech has suddenly flipped on the AI jobs wipeout scenario
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “The sentiment change isn’t limited to tech leaders: A survey by EY-Parthenon found that the percentage of CEOs who believe AI investments will result in significant reductions in head count fell from around 46% in January 2025 to just 20% this May.”

item.title: Google’s AI buildout drove 37% increase in electricity use in 2025
item.description: Ars Technica: “Google reported that its annual electricity consumption rose by 37 percent in 2025—the largest increase in the company’s history as Silicon Valley’s AI data center buildout continues. But the tech giant says it kept operational carbon emissions down by continuing to purchase massive amounts of clean energy.”

item.title: Tilly Norwood, AI ‘actor’ denounced by actors union, to star in feature film
item.description: NBC News: “The feature film will be a comedy-drama called ‘Misaligned,’ and it will star Tilly Norwood in a ‘hybrid production with traditional film and TV professionals — such as directors, writers and editors — working alongside AI specialists, with AI training and mentorship built into the production itself,’ the company said.”

item.title: When AI hurts people, who’s to blame? Global experts grapple with accountability
item.description: United Nations: “Who is legally responsible when Artificial Intelligence causes harm? The issue took centre stage on Tuesday – day two of the first ever UN summit on AI governance, where leading experts warned of mounting evidence of human rights violations linked to the revolutionary technology.”

item.title: A new attack uses a BioShock-style puzzle to convince AI browsers they’re not in the real world
item.description: TechSpot: “Researchers from LayerX recently unveiled BioShocking, a new type of vulnerability designed to target AI-powered browsers capable of executing autonomous tasks on the open web. The security firm explained that BioShocking can ‘game’ an AI-based browser, causing the system to execute malicious instructions after effectively bypassing its intended security guardrails.”

item.title: Google AI Overviews Study Finds Lost Clicks Weren’t Lower Quality
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “An updated AI Overviews experiment finds no measurable difference in bounce rates, time on site, or returns to search between clicks with and without summaries.”

item.title: COrigami – an AI-based Origami Design Tool
item.description: Origami by Michał Kosmulski: “I’m very excited to announce a paper I have co-authored: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami. It introduces COrigami, a first of its kind AI-based origami design tool, capable of generating origami crease patterns and simulating their folded look, including simple shaping, starting from a textual description.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The Plains to Peaks Collective Launches a New Discovery Platform
item.description: Wyoming State Library: “The Colorado State Library, in partnership with the Wyoming State Library, is excited to announce the launch of a brand-new Plains to Peaks Collective site (plains2peaks.org) for searching historic collections across Colorado and Wyoming.”

item.title: Tinfoil Pigeons
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: From the About section on the front page: “Every airliner, cargo hauler, helicopter and suspiciously quiet turboprop broadcasts its position over ADS-B, and our scope listens. Enter a postcode or town — anywhere in the world — or use your location, and the flights overhead appear as blips, sweep after sweep, exactly where they really are.”

item.title: California releases CalEnviroScreen 5.0 to identify and prioritize pollution-burdened communities, announces preliminary disadvantaged communities designation
item.description: State of California: “The Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) today released CalEnviroScreen 5.0, an update to the state’s mapping tool that identifies communities hardest hit by multiple pollution sources. Combining data from multiple environmental, health and socioeconomic indicators, the state has used CalEnviroScreen to focus resources and environmental protection actions where they are needed most.”

item.title: Fabrice Canel, Longtime Bing Search Leader, Retires From Microsoft
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Canel led the Bing team responsible for crawling and indexing the web, and he was closely associated with Bing Webmaster Tools. He also became the public face of IndexNow, the open protocol Microsoft Bing announced with Yandex in 2021 for notifying search engines about new and updated pages.”

item.title: Google Maps is restoring the names of locations in Poland that were changed to offensive alternatives
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Polish news network TVPWorld reported on the matter, with examples including the Presidential Palace being renamed ‘Hooligans’ Palace,’ the Warsaw Uprising Museum becoming ‘Museum of the Third Reich Uprising,’ and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier becoming ‘Tomb of the Known SS Soldier.’ Screenshots of some of the altered names were shared on social media.”

item.title: Wordle, but for art history—Anthropeum turns the Met Museum into an online game
item.description: Scientific American: “Armchair art historians, rejoice: there’s a free online daily game just for you. Called Anthropeum, the game involves guessing where and when various artifacts from New York City’s Metropolitan Museum of Art come from.”

item.title: The Human Story of the Open Web
item.description: Jeffrey Zeldman: “The new digital landowner class can also take away our favorite software, or change it in ways to which we never consented. The answer to this destruction of our shared digital commons by a handful of billionaires is the same as it has always been: own your content on the open web (your domain on a server, like mine on this one), and replace proprietary software with open source alternatives.”

item.title: If you use Google, you’re training its AI. Here’s how to opt out.
item.description: TechCrunch: “Consider this a belated PSA: A recent change to Google’s privacy settings is allowing the company to store more of your data, including media such as ‘images, files, and audio and video recordings,’ to improve its AI models. In other words, if you upload any media to Google’s Search services, it’s being used to train AI unless you opt out.”

item.title: Musk’s X poses “serious risk to Americans’ privacy,” advocates warn FTC
item.description: Ars Technica: “Ahead of a July 2 deadline to submit public comments, advocates are warning the Federal Trade Commission that it must keep close watch over Elon Musk’s X and firmly reject a recent bid to end the agency’s ongoing audits of the platform’s data handling.”

item.title: Threads’ ubiquitous Mr Beast spam is part of a massive crypto scam network
item.description: Engadget: “A spam account replies to a popular post with a nonsensical phrase and a low-quality screenshot of the British newspaper The Times featuring a fictitious story about Mr Beast. There’s usually a second, seemingly random, image — often a bouquet of flowers with an iPhone. The formula has some minor variations, but these posts are absolutely everywhere. Like so much spam on social media, it’s part of a massive crypto scam.”

item.title: There May Be Three Times as Many Insect Species as Previously Thought
item.description: University of Connecticut: “Most experts have currently accepted an estimate of about 6 million insect species, an appraisal that has stood for the last 40 years. But the new count, which used genetic information for 1.6 million individual tropical insects, a census of a highly diverse group of parasitic wasps in Costa Rica, and statistical strategies, conservatively estimates the total number of insect species at closer to 14 to 20 million.”

item.title: Could the clean energy revolution be powered by wastewater?
item.description: Northeastern University: “The researchers found that enough magnesium, lithium, uranium, titanium, fluorine and silicon could be recovered from wastewaters to meet at least one-tenth of each resource’s projected demand in the international clean energy sector.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New archives bring New Brunswick’s hidden queer history online
item.description: CBC: “The Queer Heritage Initiative of New Brunswick has launched a new website this week, bringing together more than a decade of archival work documenting LGBTQ+ life across the province.”

item.title: Vaccination rates in Texas schools have been dropping. Look up the latest vaccination rates in your district.
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Each school year, Texas public school districts and private schools report to the state vaccination rates for each immunization required to attend kindergarten and 7th grade. The state publishes spreadsheets with information from these reports. The Texas Tribune has made this publicly available data easily searchable. Find those coverage rates for the 2025-26 school year with the change from the previous year below.”

item.title: NYC Department of City Planning Launches NYC Language Explorer, a New Interactive Tool Mapping Languages Spoken Across the Five Boroughs
item.description: City of New York: “Offering detailed information on the most commonly spoken languages at the citywide, borough and Community District levels, as well as statistics for additional language groups, the tool provides a powerful new way to examine the city’s rich linguistic diversity and better understand local language service needs.”

item.title: Discovery Center’s Historic Photo Archive online, open to public
item.description: Columbia Gorge News: “Columbia Gorge Discovery Center and Museum has restored their Historic Photo Archives online…Thanks to a grant from the City of The Dalles, the public now can view more than 30,600 images from the museum’s vast photo collection.”

item.title: Former Microsoft dev built a 2.5KB Notepad clone with zero AI features
item.description: TechSpot: “[Dave] Plummer is the man who claims to have created some major Windows features, including the original Task Manager application. Now, the YouTuber and retired developer shared his latest creation: a text editor named TinyRetroPad, which is designed to mimic Notepad’s text editing functionality while staying as small as possible on disk.”

item.title: VR and gaming are adding a kick to taekwondo
item.description: Associated Press: “Competitors wear VR headsets that transport them into a digital 3D arena, and strap motion-tracking sensors on their spine, thighs and shins. They use their bodies to control digital avatars in noncontact virtual matches, where every fast and well-timed strike depletes the opponent’s virtual health bar.”

item.title: Grim New Details From the Life of the Plaintiff in Social Media’s ‘Big Tobacco’ Case
item.description: Gizmodo: “K.G.M., the profile says, was a working class child of a fairly recent divorce when she started using YouTube, and was obsessed with her older sister who was careening toward an eating disorder. She was struggling in school. It’s familiar, and so is the idea of coping with heavy use of YouTube.”

item.title: $40 million for 9/11 document discovery, release included in city budget
item.description: The Chief: “The city will devote $34.2 million in the coming fiscal year to creating a public online portal to post documents related to post-9/11 air quality and health risks as part of the $125.8 billion Fiscal Year 2027 city budget announced June 30. Also included in the finalized budget is $6.25 million for the city’s Department of Investigation, $4 million of which will go towards completing the City Council-mandated inquiry into documents maintained by agencies across the city government from the period after 9/11.”

item.title: How a Twitter Post Discovered a New Wasp Species to Japan
item.description: Nautilus: “In 2018, insect enthusiast and author Kanji Toyosaki posted a photo to Twitter (now X) of a tiny wasp laying its eggs on a praying mantis’ egg case. The photo caught the attention of Japanese entomologist Taisuke Kawano of the Kyushu University Museum, who formally described the male of the species (Eupelmus curvator) for the first time in the journal Travaux du Muséum National d’Histoire Naturelle ‘Grigore Antipa.'”

item.title: Sound archive to be safeguarded thanks to university funding
item.description: Shropshire Council: “The collections include local radio archives, oral history interviews, and music recordings. The recordings frequently capture the memories and experiences of people and communities who are underrepresented in the archival record. They include memories of local industries, rural life, the natural world, and the experiences of people and communities who have made the Midlands their home. During the next year, an initial 1,200 recordings will be digitised and preserved. A range of events and learning activities will take place across the region, designed to showcase this important heritage.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Lehigh Valley art collection joins College of Arts and Architecture’s digital archives
item.description: Penn State: “Penn State Lehigh Valley’s historic art collection is the newest addition to the Penn State College of Arts and Architecture’s digital archives, a platform designed to preserve and provide access to collections from visual centers across Penn State.”

item.title: Victorian poet’s archive made available online
item.description: BBC: “Dorset dialect poet William Barnes bequeathed his writings, woodcuts and engravings to the county museum that he co-founded in 1846. The William Barnes Society raised £35,000 to catalogue the collection so it could be accessed anywhere in the world.”

item.title: Germany’s massive 60,000-game preservation project collapses after €1.5 million funding dries up — world’s largest game archive was entirely publicly available, now abandoned just as Sony kills physical media
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “The Internationale Computerspielesammlung (ICS), a German effort to assemble the world’s largest publicly accessible video game archive, is being wound down after roughly €1.5 million in public funding expired at the end of April and the federal government declined to renew it. GamesWirtschaft reported on July 3rd that the project’s shareholders voted unanimously to shut it down, leaving the future of its database of more than 60,000 cataloged titles unresolved.”

item.title: YouTube harkens back to original Instagram with photo post update
item.description: Tubefilter: “When you open up the YouTube Shorts app, you might not expect to see many photo posts in your feed, but YouTube wants to make those still images more common. An update to photo posts will bring snippets of licensed pop music to those pieces of content.”

item.title: Trump admin deletes cooling advice after right goes scorched on Mamdani for same info
item.description: Mediaite: “The U.S. Department of Energy apparently deleted its longstanding guidance that homeowners keep their air conditioning set to 78 degrees, after critics slammed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) for giving the exact same advice during the current heat wave.”

item.title: Presidency trains over 100 Northern influencers to counter fake news
item.description: Vanguard (Nigeria): “The Office of the Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Media and Public Enlightenment, Mr Abdulaziz Abdulaziz, has trained over 100 social media influencers from across Northern Nigeria on the effective use of social media. Speaking during the training on Sunday in Kano, Abdulaziz said the workshop was organised to equip influencers with the skills to counter disinformation and misinformation.”

item.title: Fake DMCA Complaints Keep Erasing Real Pages From Google – What To Watch For
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Copyright complaints can remove live pages from Google search before the dispute is resolved. Here’s how the takedown process works and how to spot it.”

item.title: Brazil Google notice targets YouTube betting channels
item.description: Lapaas Voice: “Brazil Google notice is the latest move by Brazil to curb illegal online betting. A notice is a formal government warning. In this case, officials told Google they were concerned about YouTube profiles that seemed to promote gambling sites not cleared to work in Brazil.”

item.title: Kansas records conflict could be handled more smoothly by an open government advisory board
item.description: Kansas Reflector: “Taxpayers should not be on the hook simply because state law creates an unresolved conflict of interest for the body enforcing not only KORA but also its companion, the Kansas Open Meetings Act. Rather, the law should empower the agency enforcing those laws to be free to construe them liberally and enforce them rigorously, not give it an excuse to bow out. Other states solve this problem in part by establishing an open government advisory board, which includes members of the public.”

item.title: How buying a washing machine became an AI comedy: Why the AI customer service revolution is a failure
item.description: Lookout Santa Cruz: “In too many cases, AI is deployed less to improve service than to create a barrier between customers and the people who could actually help them. The result is a system that saves businesses money while shifting costs onto customers.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: UVU helped digitize America’s birth certificate, bringing its drafting to life
item.description: KUER: “Given today’s technology, the idea of writing the Declaration of Independence with quill pens on parchment paper seems daunting. But that’s what the scribe charged with the task had at his disposal in 1776. It’s also why a collaboration between Utah Valley University and Pembroke College at Oxford University is called the ‘Quill Project.’ They’ve developed an interactive digital model that maps the intricate, step-by-step process of drafting the declaration.”

item.title: Indie Web Database
item.description: Petrapixel is building an “The Indie Web Database is a collection of all things indie web. For now, we have a collection of websites, webrings and cliques. The database is a project created and managed by Petrapixel (that’s me, hi!), but contributions can come from everyone. This way, the maintenance of the database is not depended on one person, but a task of the community. This also means you should take any information with a grain of salt; While I do moderate responses and do my best to keep spam out, contributions are generally not approved before going online, only changes to existing entries are.” It launched this month but already has over 500 listings available.

item.title: Online “finfluencers” grow up
item.description: MoneySense: “The Creator Insights Forum featured a scrolling highlight reel of leading content creators, including yours truly. The forum brought financial content creators together to acknowledge the growing influence of their voices and the role they play in educating Canadian financial consumers. While regulatory considerations were discussed, the broader emphasis was on helping creators navigate the space responsibly.”

item.title: July 2nd, 2026 – Heads, tails, and an AI toggle
item.description: Kagi: “We’ve added an option to disable access to AI features in search, under settings/ai. We’re also planning to add this option to onboarding, so new users can personalise their Kagi experience from the start. It’s finally here! We believe that Kagi’s application of AI should always be useful – there when you’d like it, and never when you don’t, and always respecting your privacy.”

item.title: Online collection of historic Washington newspapers reaches a million pages
item.description: The Chronicle: “As of June 16, the Washington Digital Newspapers program has officially gathered more than a million pages from historic local newspapers in its online collection.”

item.title: PlayStation just struck a hammer blow to game preservation
item.description: Engadget: “So, that’s it then. As of 2028, game discs will be a thing of the past for PlayStation. And after previously attempting to do so five years ago — before a backlash prompted it to reverse course — Sony is finally shuttering the digital storefronts on PS3 and PlayStation Vita. It doesn’t seem like the company will back down this time.”

item.title: Trump administration’s $46 billion ‘smart wall’ races ahead on the US-Mexico border
item.description: Associated Press: “The wall is under heavy scrutiny for the billions of dollars being dedicated to it when border crossings are at their lowest in decades. Critics say the U.S. is militarizing the border as it increasingly deploys sophisticated surveillance technology to the area, impacting local communities.”

item.title: Californians can protect their personal data with one click. Help us test if it works
item.description: Cal Matters: “Starting at the beginning of this year, the California Privacy Protection Agency allowed residents of the state to sign up for the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, or DROP. The tool lets consumers send an instant request to hundreds of data brokers, asking them to delete their data and stop tracking them…. CalMatters and The Markup want to keep tabs on whether data companies comply with DROP, and that’s where we need your help.”

item.title: White House report brands Smithsonian leadership as radical activists who can’t be trusted
item.description: PBS: “A White House report brands the leadership of the Smithsonian Institution, especially at the National Museum of American History, as radical activists who cannot be trusted, indicating that President Donald Trump may be preparing to install his own team.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: How Google and AI Nearly Made a Seasoned Reporter Spiral
item.description: ProPublica: “The mystery website ended up as just a single paragraph in our story. But the larger implication is obvious: fakes, counterfeits and frauds that would have taken considerable effort to create just a few years ago can now be churned out pretty much instantly.”

item.title: Cargo thieves are now stealing millions in data center hardware, not just GPUs and consoles
item.description: TechSpot: “The AI boom may be hurting consumers, white-collar workers, and rural residents living near data centers, but it’s opened up ‘new opportunities’ for cargo thieves. Criminals are reportedly cashing in on the data center construction boom by stealing millions of dollars’ worth of server hardware, cables, and other high-value tech equipment.”

item.title: Blackstone-owned QTS abandons planned world’s largest data center campus after years of lawsuits — 2,100-acre Virginia Digital Gateway project dies over a newspaper-notice technicality
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Data center developer QTS has officially terminated plans to build a portion of the planned 2,100-acre “Digital Gateway” data center campus in Virginia, following years of legal battles with local residents and historic preservation groups.”

item.title: Viral fake AI-image shows Macron kneeling before Thai king
item.description: Euronews: “Thailand’s foreign ministry has denied a viral online claim that French President Emmanuel Macron knelt before the country’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn while presenting France’s highest state honours during the Thai monarch’s state visit to Paris.”

item.title: A New AI Tool Lets Candidates See What Chatbots Are Telling Voters
item.description: NOTUS: “In California’s gubernatorial primary, Tom Steyer had the biggest war chest in a crowded field of Democrats, spending more than $200 million out of his own pocket. But money alone wasn’t enough — he ended up placing third, falling just short in his quest to compete for November’s general election. A contributing factor, according to a case study shared with NOTUS, was the unflattering response voters were presented with when they asked artificial intelligence-powered chatbots about Steyer’s candidacy. In fact, according to most models, the billionaire was just lucky to have made it into the top three.”

item.title: Schools grapple with AI cyberbullying
item.description: Evanston Now: “Beginning July 1, the state’s definition of cyberbullying was expanded to include AI-generated digital replicas, forcing districts across Illinois to update policies and procedures. Also by July 1, the Illinois State Board of Education was required to develop statewide guidance on artificial intelligence in schools.”

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg admits the AI restructuring isn’t going all that great, report says
item.description: Mashable: “In an internal town hall on Thursday, examined by Reuters, Zuckerberg admitted that AI agents had not progressed as quickly as he had expected. Additionally, according to the report, the CEO said that Meta’s AI-related restructuring wasn’t as ‘clean’ as it could have been, and that Meta execs miscalculated the timing of the changes.”

item.title: Alibaba to ban employees from using Anthropic’s coding tool, source says
item.description: Reuters: “Chinese tech giant Alibaba (9988.HK), opens new tab has banned employees from using Anthropic’s Claude ‌Code at work after the tool drew scrutiny for features that can help identify China-linked users, according to a person familiar with the order.”

item.title: Cloudflare will filter out web crawlers that serve AI companies
item.description: Engadget: “Cloudflare has announced plans to automatically block mixed-use web crawlers that index websites for search engines and act as AI agents and trainers at the same time. The company previously offered its customers the optional ability to prevent crawlers from scraping their sites for AI chatbots, but now Cloudflare’s stance is becoming more defensive by default.”

item.title: Startup sues Palo Alto Networks’ Koi Security, saying an AI-hallucinated report falsely linked it to Chinese espionage
item.description: The Register: “The legal complaint filed against Koi Security, its researchers, and Palo Alto Networks alleges that Koi used an LLM to generate the threat report, the AI system hallucinated findings about MeetingTV, and the security shop then published those as facts in a December 30 blog.”

item.title: Improving the speed and energy-efficiency of AI agents
item.description: MIT News: “Agentic workflows are artificial intelligence-powered software systems that chain together multiple models and external tools to tackle complicated tasks, like analyzing a video and answering questions about it. But the way these highly fragmented systems are designed and deployed often causes inefficiencies that can lead to wasted computation, energy, and cost.”

item.title: Why AI believes Crimea is Russian — and what to do about it
item.description: Kyiv Independent: “I work in Silicon Valley, where I create AI products every day. A few months ago, I needed an interactive map of Europe. This is a fairly simple task that requires only a few lines of code or a one-sentence prompt in a code-generation tool like Claude. As an engineer, I care about scalability, best practices, and code optimization, but as a Ukrainian, I always check whether Ukrainian sovereignty is represented correctly, and seeing Ukraine without Crimea was a turning point for me.”

item.title: Artificial intelligence chatbots adopt human power dynamics and social biases in conversations
item.description: PsyPost: “Large language models tend to adopt the social biases of human hierarchies when they are assigned different professional roles. New research shows that these artificial intelligence systems mimic behaviors like harmful compliance and authority bias, which provides evidence that power dynamics impact both the safety and realism of automated agents.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: WHO launches first global database on the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections
item.description: World Health Organization: “The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new global database on the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The open-access database is the first global platform to provide consolidated, standardized and quality-assured STI prevalence data from low- and middle-income countries from 2010 onwards.”

item.title: National Museum of Asian Art Renews Partnership With National Institute of Japanese Literature, Expands Digital Access to Rare Books
item.description: Smithsonian: “Signed this spring, the renewal is paired with the launch of a new digital resource developed in partnership with the museum: the Japanese language version of an online, searchable catalog of rare Japanese texts from the museum’s Pulverer Collection.”

item.title: The Legacy of 25 Years of Creative Commons
item.description: Creative Commons: “We are thrilled to recap the first in our series of 25th anniversary events, celebrating some of the most notable moments in the history of the development and deployment of our legal tools from creation to translation; and from advocacy to adoption.”

item.title: Amazon’s Mechanical Turk to stop accepting new customers – and not even AI can save it
item.description: The Register: “Earlier this week, AWS added the Amazon SageMaker AI – Mechanical Turk service to its list of ‘Services in Maintenance’ – AWS-speak for services it will soon retire. The Mechanical Turk website also added a warning that it will ‘be closed to new customers, effective July 30, 2026. Existing users will not be impacted by this change.'”

item.title: Wireburst: RSS feeds in Discord, because email is the devil
item.description: Cruftbox: “I am constantly in Discord. I’m there for my varied communities: gaming, beekeeping, smart home, Twitch DJs, etc. It’s already where I spend a lot of my online time. So I started wondering: could a Discord bot manage RSS feeds and push new items into channels? Organized by topic, one feed per channel, there when I want to scroll through them? Turns out, yes. With some help from Claude, I built Wireburst.”

item.title: Turn Any WordPress Playground Into a Guided Education Experience
item.description: Pootlepress: “WordPress Playground makes it incredibly easy to share a complete WordPress site with a single link. But the moment someone opens it, they’re often on their own. Students don’t know where to begin. Clients are worried they’ll break something. Plugin users miss the feature you wanted them to see. Guided Tours aim to solve that problem.”

item.title: EPA sued over public records request for nitrate research
item.description: Arkansas Advocate: “The environmental group Food & Water Watch is suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for failing to supply requested information about a nitrate assessment. Food & Water Watch allege the ‘apparently scuttled’ assessment would have provided EPA with the research necessary to update drinking water standards for nitrate and nitrite.”

item.title: GoDaddy warns India’s fake website crackdown could damage the internet and privacy
item.description: Business Today: “India is cracking down on websites that impersonate established brands. However, GoDaddy, the US-based internet domain seller, argues that its new court-ordered rules against fake websites could create privacy, security, and operational problems for website owners, not just scammers.”

item.title: Goethe University to Host International Bio-Research Database
item.description: Goethe University: “Soon, an internationally networked research database at Goethe University will collect structural data on biomolecules obtained worldwide through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies. The database will complement two existing databases in the United States (the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank, BMRB) and Japan (BMRBj).”

item.title: Digital poverty is holding university students back
item.description: The Conversation: “When a student can’t submit their essay because the household’s only device is being used by three siblings for school, or because their mobile data ran out mid-lecture, they are experiencing digital poverty. Digital poverty describes a cluster of overlapping disadvantages: lack of access to devices, unreliable or unaffordable internet connectivity, and insufficient digital skills to make meaningful use of online resources even when access exists.”

item.title: A Trip Inside the World’s Largest Collection of Jumbo Perfume Bottles
item.description: Allure: “This is the passion project of Sudhir Gupta and his wife Mercedes Acosta, who have assembled nearly 4,000 jumbo bottles, or ifactices,i spanning more than 100 years of perfume history. Factices began to be produced in the late 19th century when perfume sales shifted from pharmacies to department stores.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Ancient Rome’s version of Google Maps: how long to reach the beach
item.description: Euronews: “A Dutch engineer has reconstructed, with the help of academic sources and ancient cartography, the road map that linked up the Roman Empire. The result, accessible from any browser, including on mobile phones, allows users to plot routes between cities of Antiquity and find out how many days the journey would have taken on foot or on horseback.” This is not the same as the Roman road system tool that launched last fall.

item.title: Kentucky launches domestic violence data dashboard
item.description: Spectrum News 1: “Kentucky has launched a new public dashboard that allows users to track domestic violence data by county and region, according to a news release. The dashboard also provides Kentuckians with information on shelters, support services, offenders and law enforcement outcomes.”

item.title: This Virtual Closet Lets You Browse 1,000+ Criterion Collection Films
item.description: 80LV: “The entire library of the Criterion Collection, featuring over 1000 contemporary and classic films, was transformed into a walk-in virtual closet, where you can click on the title and learn information about the film.” I took a little extra time to play with this site (my standard for anything that looks assist- or vibe-coded). It’s simple (browse the shelves, click for information, get options to stream on the Criterion Channel or buy on Amazon.) Hit F to go straight to a search form if you don’t want to browse.

item.title: 4chan’s feud with the U.K. previews the future of social media regulations
item.description: Tubefilter: “The forum and memeboard, which is infamous for hosting many types of extreme content, is ignoring a bill that has sat unpaid for more than a year. Ofcom has demanded that 4chan accept a hefty fine pursuant to the terms of the Online Safety Act, but the British telecom regulator has only received AI-generated hamsters in return.”

item.title: Vim text editor game teaches you keyboard shortcuts with ice cream delivery
item.description: The Register: “London-based developer and designer Marcus Michaels has created Vim Scoops, a simple HTML/CSS/JavaScript game that lives in a web browser to help users learn them. As an ice cream truck trying to make the most efficient deliveries to customers as possible, players use Vim motions to dart around the screen and try to meet par on each level.”

item.title: Google launches improved pronunciation tool for te reo Māori place names
item.description: Radio New Zealand: “For many years Māori place names pronounced by Google Maps have sounded kawa (unpleasant) in the ears of te reo Māori speakers. It will use a new AI-powered text-to-speech (TTS) model in English that can correctly pronounce cities and towns with te reo Māori names.”

item.title: Idaho labor economist ran anonymous accounts promoting pro-Russian, far-right views
item.description: InvestigateWest: “…online researchers recently identified [Sam] Wolkenhauer as the anonymous poster behind large Substack and X.com accounts that drive thousands of dollars in subscriptions each month with pro-Russian commentary that often traffics in Nazi imagery and amplifies far-right organizations.”

item.title: Google is investigating reports of reviews going missing and pausing reviews on local listings
item.description: Search Engine Land: “After several days of complaints from businesses, Google has confirmed it is investigating reports of missing reviews from Google Local listings and has paused the ability of Google Business Profile listings to receive reviews.”

item.title: The West can learn from Ukraine’s success against Russian propaganda
item.description: Atlantic Council: “The roots of Russian information warfare against Ukraine run deep and are part of a centuries-old battle rooted in imperial propaganda and competing civilizational narratives. Even if a ceasefire between the two countries is eventually agreed, this would not end hostilities in the cognitive sphere. Ukraine is therefore set to remain at the forefront of efforts to counter the Kremlin’s constantly evolving disinformation operations.” Good afternoon, Internet…
